title: Exploitation of host U2AF1 and U2AF2 splicing factors facilitates mosquito-borne orthoflavivirus infection across species.
data_url: https://www.iprox.cn/page/project.html?id=IPX0013687000 (mass spectrometry deposit); supplementary PDF via Europe PMC PMC13376149

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and unzipped the full Europe PMC supplement (2.8 MB): it is one 17-page PDF plus figure images, with no spreadsheet of any kind. I read every PDF page with pdfplumber. The only quantitative table is Table S6, 'List of proteins enriched in the ER of ZIKV- and DENV2-infected cells', which I counted at exactly 135 rows across pages 14-17 with 4 columns (Gene, Accession, Foldchange, Unique peptides). 24 of the 135 rows have no gene symbol ('unnamed protein product') and HSP90AB1 appears twice with different accessions and fold changes (2.80 and 2.39). Tables S1-S5 are PCR primer, sgRNA/shRNA and antibody lists, not measurements. I probed the mass spectrometry deposit (iProX IPX0013687000) four ways: the ProteomeXchange PROXI interface returned an all-null record, the iProX project page is JavaScript-only, the iProX internal project/subproject API redirects to a login server, and the ProteomeXchange GetDataset call rejected the identifier as malformed.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: That the mass spectrometry data exist and were deposited (data availability statement names iProX IPX0013687000). That the proteomics was done on endoplasmic reticulum (the membrane network where flaviviruses replicate) fractions from Dengue- or Zika-infected Huh7.5 cells. That roughly six of the enriched proteins were followed up functionally (U2AF1, U2AF2, TGM2 and a handful of others appear in the primer tables); the paper never provides a gene-level table of which candidates were proviral, antiviral or neutral.

a1_downloadable.note: Partly. The supplement PDF downloads freely and I opened it. The underlying mass spectrometry deposit (iProX IPX0013687000) could not be retrieved by any public programmatic route - PROXI returned an empty record and the iProX API redirects to a login page - so the only data I could actually open is the 135-row PDF table.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: No label column exists. The only outcome anyone would want to predict - 'is this host protein needed for flavivirus replication?' - is nowhere in the files; it would have to be constructed from each gene's individual knockdown figure, and only about six genes were tested at all. The fold-change column is an enrichment measurement, not the biological outcome.

a3_inputs_present.note: Inputs would be protein sequences, which are not in the files but are one-to-one resolvable from the 111 named NCBI accessions (e.g. NP_006749); 24 rows have no usable identifier.

a4_units_stated.note: Column headers state 'Foldchange' (ratio, infected ER fraction over mock) and 'Unique peptides' (count), seen in the PDF table; the normalisation behind the ratio is not described.

a5_enough_rows.note: 135 rows counted by hand in Table S6, against a checklist floor of ~1,500 for regression or ~400 for classification. Worse, all 135 are positives (proteins above the enrichment cutoff); the non-enriched remainder of the proteome was never released, so there is no negative class either.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~50 KB of extracted table text; 2.2 MB PDF
a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially small. Size was never the problem here.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The paper text gives no candidate count to contradict, so nothing disagrees; but that also means the 135 rows cannot be cross-checked against any stated number.

a8_label_provenance.note: There is no label to trace. If the fold-change column were used as the target instead, it is a single-replicate enrichment ratio from one experiment in one cell line with no replicate structure shown, and predicting it from the same proteins' sequences would be predicting abundance in one mass spectrometry run, not biology.

existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved - I saw only the search listing and title, so I am recording no number.

existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved - search listing only, no number recorded.

backbone.name: ESM-2 (a protein language model with small CPU-runnable checkpoints)
backbone.hardware: Laptop CPU would be ample for 135 sequences, which is itself the problem - 135 examples cannot train or honestly evaluate any head.
backbone.licence: ESM-2 is MIT-licensed; the paper's supplement carries the article's Creative Commons licence.

integration.partner_dataset: Published genome-wide CRISPR knockout screens for Zika and Dengue host factors, plus UniProt/AlphaFold DB, joinable on gene symbol or UniProt accession.
integration.join_key: Gene symbol / NCBI protein accession, resolvable to UniProt
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does being enriched at the endoplasmic reticulum during infection predict being functionally required for infection in CRISPR screens? - a real question, but answering it needs the screens' labels and a full proteome background, neither of which this paper provides.

controls.positive_control: U2AF1, U2AF2 and RACK1, all in Table S6 and all independently reported as flavivirus-required, would have to rank high in any model.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling would be meaningless at n=135 with no negative class.
controls.external_validation: Published Zika/Dengue CRISPR screens and the BioGRID/IntAct virus-host interaction records exist, but they would supply the labels this dataset lacks rather than validate it.

honest_claim_h3: At best: 'among 135 proteins that one laboratory found enriched at the endoplasmic reticulum in one infected liver cell line, this model ranks their enrichment ratio' - which is a claim about one mass spectrometry run, not about flavivirus biology.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a protein's sequence to predict whether a mosquito-borne virus needs that human protein to replicate.
plain_idea.train_on: The project I considered would train on the paper's only table: 135 human proteins enriched at the endoplasmic reticulum in Zika- or Dengue-infected liver cells, each with a fold-change and a peptide count (counted in the file).
plain_idea.predict: Whether knocking the protein out blocks viral replication. That true answer comes from individual laboratory knockdown experiments, and the paper ran them for only about six of the 135 proteins.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Antiviral drug hunters would like to shortlist host proteins worth targeting instead of running genome-wide screens; but with 135 positives-only rows and no outcome column, nothing here can support that.

ml_idea: Considered and abandoned: rank human proteins by how likely they are to be a required flavivirus host factor, from sequence embeddings, using this paper's endoplasmic-reticulum enrichment list as labels. It dies because the enrichment list is 135 positives with no negatives and no functional outcome column; the mechanistic half of the paper (domain mapping of U2AF1/U2AF2, mosquito homolog swaps) is a handful of western blots and plaque assays, which is biology but not a dataset.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed beyond the PDF parse itself: 135 sequences through a small ESM-2 checkpoint is minutes on a CPU. Every compute number here is tiny, which only underlines that the shortage is data, not hardware.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the rows in Table S6 and ask how many have a measured proviral/antiviral outcome. Answer: 135 rows, ~6 outcomes. That took ten minutes and ends the project.

verdict_reason: Fails A2, A5 and A8. The supplement is a single PDF whose only measurement table has 135 rows, all above an enrichment cutoff so there are no negatives, 24 rows lack a gene identifier and one gene is duplicated with disagreeing values. The outcome anyone would predict - whether a host protein is needed for infection - is not a column and was measured for only about six genes. The mass spectrometry deposit (iProX IPX0013687000) could not be opened through any public programmatic route, and even if it could, it would be raw spectra rather than a feature/label table. Excellent mechanistic virology; not a machine learning dataset.
